definitions.definition: How well a theory or idea explains the facts we observe.
definitions.example: If a theory explains why apples fall and planets orbit, it has high explanatory power.

definitions.definition: The belief that only natural laws and forces exist, and nothing supernatural.
definitions.example: Naturalism says there is no God, no soul, only matter and energy.

definitions.definition: The belief in a personal God who created and sustains the universe.
definitions.example: Christianity, Islam, and Judaism are theistic religions.

definitions.definition: The argument that God allows evil because free will requires the possibility of choosing wrong.
definitions.example: If you can only choose good, you're not really free — like a video game with only one path.

definitions.definition: An argument that is logically consistent, even if it doesn't feel satisfying.
definitions.example: A math proof can be structurally coherent even if the answer is surprising.

definitions.definition: Suffering that seems to have no good reason or purpose.
definitions.example: A child dying of cancer for no apparent reason is often called gratuitous evil.

definitions.definition: Specific discoveries that would completely disprove a theory or argument.
definitions.example: If someone finds a fossil that breaks evolution, that's a kill condition for Darwin's theory.

definitions.definition: Claiming a text predicted something after the fact, not before.
definitions.example: Saying a prophecy was written after the event happened, not before.

definitions.definition: How life could arise from non-living chemicals without any outside help.
definitions.example: Scientists are trying to create life in a lab from simple molecules.

definitions.definition: Someone who believes only physical matter exists, not mind or spirit.
definitions.example: A materialist thinks thoughts are just brain chemicals, not a soul.

definitions.definition: The mystery of why we have subjective experiences (like feeling pain or seeing red) at all.
definitions.example: We know which brain areas light up when you see red, but not why you actually experience 'redness'.

definitions.definition: The raw feeling of right and wrong, like guilt or moral approval.
definitions.example: That gut feeling you get when you know you did something wrong.

definitions.definition: When different lines of evidence point to the same conclusion.
definitions.example: If eyewitnesses, fingerprints, and DNA all point to the same suspect, that's convergence.

definitions.definition: A measure of how incredibly unlikely the universe's low-entropy (ordered) start was, calculated by Roger Penrose.
definitions.example: The odds of the universe starting so ordered are like flipping a coin and getting heads a trillion trillion times in a row.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system.
definitions.example: A messy room has high entropy; a tidy room has low entropy.

definitions.definition: Eugene Wigner, a physicist who wrote about the 'unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics' in describing nature.
definitions.example: Wigner was amazed that abstract math, invented in someone's head, perfectly describes how planets move.

definitions.definition: Kurt Gödel, a mathematician who proved that any sufficiently complex system has true statements that cannot be proven within that system.
definitions.example: Gödel showed that math can never be completely self-proving — there will always be unprovable truths.

definitions.definition: Body feelings (like a knot in your stomach) that help guide decision-making, studied by Antonio Damasio.
definitions.example: That uneasy feeling you get before making a risky choice is a somatic marker.

definitions.definition: A measure of information content or uncertainty, used in communication theory.
definitions.example: A coin flip has high Shannon entropy because it's unpredictable; a boring speech has low entropy.

definitions.definition: The observation that the universe's physical constants are set to incredibly precise values for life to exist.
definitions.example: If gravity were slightly stronger, the universe would have collapsed immediately after the Big Bang.

definitions.definition: Basic assumptions that are accepted without proof, from which other truths are derived.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.
definitions.first_appearance: We set the rules in Chapter One.

definitions.definition: A claim that cannot be proven false, no matter what evidence is presented.
definitions.example: Saying 'invisible unicorns exist' is unfalsifiable because you can't prove they don't.
definitions.first_appearance: We set the rules in Chapter One.

definitions.definition: A list of old scientific theories that were once accepted but later replaced.
definitions.example: The idea that the sun goes around the Earth is in the paradigm graveyard.

definitions.definition: An inborn sense of right and wrong that all humans seem to have.
definitions.example: Even babies prefer helpful characters over mean ones, showing a built-in judgment layer.

definitions.definition: Latin for 'out of nothing' — the idea that God created the universe from nothing.
definitions.example: Creation ex nihilo means God didn't use any pre-existing materials.
definitions.first_appearance: Phenomenon table: Origin of the Universe

definitions.definition: Something that exists by its own nature, not caused by anything else.
definitions.example: God is said to be self-existent, while everything else depends on something else for its existence.
definitions.first_appearance: Phenomenon table: Origin of the Universe

definitions.definition: The building blocks of DNA that pair up to form the genetic code.
definitions.example: A, T, C, and G are the four letters of DNA base pairs.

definitions.definition: A system that can detect and fix mistakes in data, like DNA's ability to repair itself.
definitions.example: Your phone uses error-correcting codes to fix garbled text messages.

definitions.definition: The process where organisms better adapted to their environment survive and reproduce more.
definitions.example: Giraffes with longer necks can reach more leaves, so they survive better and pass on long-neck genes.

definitions.definition: Brain activity patterns that are linked to specific mental experiences.
definitions.example: When you feel happy, certain brain areas light up — those are neural correlates of happiness.
definitions.first_appearance: Phenomenon table: Hard Problem of Consciousness

definitions.definition: The first-person, inner feeling of being you — like what it's like to taste chocolate.
definitions.example: A robot can detect chocolate, but it doesn't have the subjective experience of tasting it.
definitions.first_appearance: Phenomenon table: Hard Problem of Consciousness

definitions.definition: The mystery of why abstract mathematics, invented in the human mind, so perfectly describes the physical universe.
definitions.example: It's like if you made up a board game and then discovered the rules exactly match how the solar system works.

definitions.definition: An immediate sense of right and wrong, without needing to think about it.
definitions.example: You don't need a rulebook to know that pushing someone down is wrong — that's moral intuition.

definitions.definition: An evolutionary advantage that increases the chance of having offspring.
definitions.example: Being strong might give a reproductive payoff because it helps you compete for mates.

definitions.definition: An attempt to explain why a good God allows evil and suffering.
definitions.example: The free will defense is one type of theodicy.
definitions.first_appearance: I don't have a clean answer for this.

definitions.definition: Latin for 'privation of good' — the idea that evil is not a thing itself, but the absence of something good that should be there.
definitions.example: Darkness isn't a thing; it's just the absence of light. Evil is like that — the absence of good.
definitions.first_appearance: I don't have a clean answer for this.

definitions.definition: A reasoned defense of a belief, especially religious faith.
definitions.example: A Christian apologetic might argue that the resurrection of Jesus is historically credible.
definitions.first_appearance: I don't have a clean answer for this.

definitions.definition: Ancient Jewish manuscripts discovered in caves near the Dead Sea, dating from around 250 BC to 68 AD.
definitions.example: The Dead Sea Scrolls contain some of the oldest copies of the Hebrew Bible.

definitions.definition: Physical copies of ancient texts that help scholars determine when and how they were written.
definitions.example: Comparing different manuscript copies helps figure out if a text was changed over time.

definitions.definition: A theory's ability to correctly forecast future observations or discoveries.
definitions.example: Einstein's theory of relativity had predictive power because it predicted that light would bend around stars.

definitions.definition: Software that is permanently stored in a device, controlling its basic functions.
definitions.example: The BIOS in a computer is firmware — it's built-in and runs when you turn the computer on.

definitions.definition: The individual, subjective experiences of sensations like redness, pain, or sweetness.
definitions.example: The 'redness' of a rose is a quale (singular of qualia) — it's the feeling of seeing red.

definitions.definition: The argument that two things share the same underlying structure or pattern.
definitions.example: Saying that a spiral galaxy and a whirlpool have the same shape is a structural identity claim.

definitions.definition: The underlying material or foundation on which something exists or operates.
definitions.example: Soil is the substrate for plants; silicon is the substrate for computer chips.
definitions.first_appearance: We proved that evil can't come first.
